title: "Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations"

[Lecture slides](../lectures/09-rmarkdown/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](09-rmarkdown-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)


## Today's question

Can someone read our explanation, inspect our calculation, and see the figure
without copying results manually? An **R Markdown report** combines ordinary text
with executable R code. Rendering turns that source document into a readable HTML
report. An HTML report can be opened in a browser; the editable source ends in
`.Rmd` and should be kept too.

These course webpages are built with Quarto. Your reports use R Markdown. You do
not need to create a Quarto document or learn a second report system.

## Open the supplied template

Open the project and then `report.Rmd` from its root folder. First save an
unchanged backup if you want one. Keep your working `.Rmd` at the project root so
that `data/seedlings.csv` points to the supplied data. Moving it into `reports/`
would change the relative location of the data during an ordinary knit.

The template has a short header between `---` lines, including a title and
`output: html_document`. That header configures the document. Leave the output
format unchanged for now. A heading in ordinary text starts with `#`, while a
code comment starting with `#` lives inside a code chunk. Their location matters.

Here is a minimal complete report. The three-backtick fences in the box belong
in your `.Rmd` file.

<pre><code>---
title: "Seedling growth"
output: html_document
---

## Question

How much did the seedlings grow during the observation period?

&#96;&#96;&#96;{r import}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings &lt;- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings &lt;- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
&#96;&#96;&#96;

There are &#96;r nrow(seedlings)&#96; plants in the dataset.

&#96;&#96;&#96;{r mean-growth}
mean(seedlings$growth_mm)
&#96;&#96;&#96;

Growth is final minus initial length, measured in millimetres.
</code></pre>

The fences mark where an R **chunk** starts and ends. Chunk labels such as `import` are names
for sections of code and must be unique within a report. The inline expression
in the sentence inserts a calculated result into prose; R executes it during
rendering. You can begin with ordinary prose and add inline calculations later.

## Render, rather than assembling results by hand

Save the source, then choose **Knit**. Rendering runs the chunks in document
order and creates an HTML file. For an explicit equivalent command from the R
Console, use the following command. Do not put it inside `report.Rmd`: a report
must not try to render itself.

```{r}
rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")
```

`rmarkdown::render` calls a function in the `rmarkdown` package without loading
all of that package's functions. Its `output_dir` puts the rendered result in
`reports/`; the `.Rmd` stays at the project root. The Knit button may initially
put its HTML next to the source instead. Both are HTML reports; locate the
actual file rather than assuming it appeared in a particular folder.

A report must contain its imports and calculations. An object you created only
in the Console may let a chunk run interactively, yet be absent during knitting.
The saved source must be sufficient to rebuild the result from the saved data.

## Add a figure and its meaning

In your report, load `ggplot2` and reuse the growth plot from day 8. Give the
figure a caption by starting its chunk with this line:

<pre><code>&#96;&#96;&#96;{r growth-figure, fig.cap="Each point represents one independently potted seedling."}
# Put the plotting code here.
&#96;&#96;&#96;
</code></pre>

Replace the comment with the plotting code, keeping both chunk fences. Write a sentence below the figure
explaining what the vertical axis measures. A caption identifies what a figure
shows; the surrounding text explains why it matters. Code can be visible in this
first report so that your method is easy to inspect.

## Exercises

1. Render the supplied template before changing it. Confirm the HTML opens.
2. Change its title, question, and author information; save and render again.
3. Put the import, growth calculation, and labelled plot in chunks in the right
   order. Remove repeated chunks that create the same object unnecessarily.
4. Add methods explaining what one row represents and how growth was calculated.
5. Deliberately misspell a column name, render, and read the error's chunk name.
   Fix the spelling and render successfully. Practise recovery, not memorisation.
6. Restart R and render the document again using the command above.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: rendering stops

Read the first useful error and its chunk label. Check that the document loads
packages before using their functions, imports the data before calculating, and
uses the exact filename and column names. Check every chunk has an opening and
closing fence. Ask for help with the error text; never attach passwords.
:::


## Make and diagnose a small complete report

Save a root-level copy of the starter as `report-workshop.Rmd`. Make deliberate
errors in this copy, record their messages and repairs, and restore a successful
render after each.

1. Add a sentence describing the input file, simulated study, independent unit,
   and growth calculation. Read the report in source form and identify which
   parts are ordinary prose, chunk fences, R instructions, and header settings.
   A heading outside a chunk is not an R comment, even if both start with `#`.
2. Keep the import/preparation before the plot. Add an inline result displaying
   the number of input plants, using the pattern already shown in the lesson.
   Render with Knit, then find that number in the HTML and identify the code
   that produced it. Keep installation commands out of the report.
3. Give every chunk a unique descriptive label. In the disposable workshop copy,
   deliberately give two chunks the same label and attempt a render. Read the
   error, record it in `reports/render-recovery.txt`, then restore unique labels.
4. Deliberately misspell the CSV filename in the import, render, and record the
   first useful error. Check the project location and actual filename, then fix
   the spelling. Notice that an object left over in the Console does not make
   a wrong saved import path correct.
5. Move a plot chunk above the chunk creating its derived variable, render,
   and explain the dependency error. Restore the correct order and render
   successfully. Record which object must exist before the plotting instruction.
   When comparing errors, change one cause at a time.
6. Reopen the HTML in a browser after a successful render. Compare it with the
   `.Rmd`: which is the editable recipe, which is the reading copy, and where
   are the actual measurements? Close and reopen the project, restart R, and
   knit again without first running analysis commands manually in the Console.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: record a small reproducible failure, not a screenshot alone

For each experiment write the changed line or chunk label, exact first useful
error, diagnosis, repair, and successful check. A screenshot may support that
record, but the saved source is needed to investigate code. Render using Knit
or the Console.
:::

## Switch inputs without leaving misleading prose

Create `transfer-report.Rmd` at the project root with **Save
As**, leaving the workshop source intact. It will describe the eighteen-plant
`data/seedlings-transfer.csv` study: independent pots, nine allocated to each
group, lengths in mm measured seven days apart. This is another simulated study,
not evidence about a real plant treatment. Use only skills already taught.

1. Replace the imported filename and use a consistent object name for that
   table. Include all library calls, import, and growth calculation in the
   report. Check dimensions, labels, and missing counts rather than relying on
   the template's earlier 24-plant result.
2. Update the question, methods, caption, and any manually written sample-size
   text. Use an inline calculation for the total row count so the number is
   tied to the imported table. A report with a new figure but an old dataset
   description mixes two different studies.
3. Add the initial-versus-final plot and the individual-growth-by-group plot
   from your saved day 8 transfer script. Identify the vertical quantity in each
   caption. You may use the reference pattern rather than reconstructing every
   plotting option from memory. State what one point represents.
4. Describe what you observe, identify a question the plots cannot settle,
   and state a limitation.
5. Render from a fresh session, locate the produced HTML, and check that the
   caption, figures, inline count, input name, and prose all describe this same
   study. Search your source for the old filename and the number 24; investigate
   any remaining occurrence instead of assuming it is harmless.
6. Copy the source, `introcomputing.Rproj`, and required `data` inputs into a
   practice project folder, keeping relative locations. Include `output` and
   `reports` folders if your code writes there. Open that copy's `.Rproj` and
   render from its root. Record any missing dependency in `render-recovery.txt`.
   This tests whether the project works from another location on your laptop.

**Check and retain:** the transfer report describes 18 plants, nine per group,
with no missing initial/final lengths; T01 grew 15.0 mm. Keep both `.Rmd` sources,
their HTML outputs, and the recovery log. The same workflow now has two deliberately
separate input files and two narratives that must not be mixed accidentally.


## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Which files do you keep?

Keep the `.Rmd` source, its input data, and the generated HTML. HTML is convenient
for reading; it does not replace the source needed to update the analysis.
Changing a number in the prose by hand would break the link to its calculation.
:::

**Keep:** your saved `report.Rmd` and a successfully rendered HTML report.
